criterion: Role-based access control enforced for all Record endpoints
supabase_justification: Verified via automated pytest suite (test_authorization.py, 12/12 passing, Section 5) confirming org-scoped RLS policies block cross-org access on list/create/read/update paths.
django_justification: Same pytest suite plus 4/4 Django unit tests; permission classes + get_queryset() filtering enforce org scoping on all endpoints.

criterion: Passwords/credentials never logged or exposed in API responses
Data can be exported in a non-proprietary format without provider tooling
Underlying schema/business logic is inspectable and modifiable
File uploads validated for type and size before storage
Database can be migrated without vendor-proprietary extensions
supabase_justification: Supabase's managed Postgres does install several platform extensions by default (pgsodium, pg_graphql, pg_net, wrappers, vault), but this project's actual schema (organisations/profiles/records/file_uploads, RLS via SECURITY DEFINER functions) uses none of them — confirmed in the schema-review finding at row 81. The schema itself is portable to any plain Postgres instance.
django_justification: Vanilla postgres:16 image, no extensions used beyond core PostgreSQL/Django ORM features.

criterion: CRUD operations on Records complete correctly for all defined fields
Reporting/aggregate query (report_view) returns results scoped to caller's organisation only
supabase_justification: Initial implementation leaked all orgs' rows because Postgres views execute as owner by default; fixed via ALTER VIEW ... SET (security_invoker = true), re-verified live (single scoped row returned instead of all 50).
django_justification: report_view is a plain Django queryset filtered by the caller's org via get_queryset(); scoping verified directly.

criterion: System behaves correctly at organisation-data boundary (no cross-org leakage) under concurrent writes
API accepts and correctly processes the full documented set of query parameters/filters
Partial/incomplete request payloads are rejected with a clear validation error, not a 500
supabase_justification: POST with an empty body ({}) is correctly rejected (403), but via a raw RLS policy violation ('new row violates row-level security policy for table records', code 42501) rather than a clear field-level message like 'org_id is required.' Rejection behaviour is correct/secure, but the error is not developer-friendly — it exposes internal policy machinery instead of naming the missing field.
django_justification: POST /records/ with an empty body ({}) returned 201 Created, not a validation error — model defaults silently filled in (status='open', payload={}). Arguably worse than Supabase's confusing-but-correct rejection: an empty/incomplete submission is accepted as if it were valid rather than rejected at all.

criterion: Duplicate/idempotent create requests are handled predictably (no silent duplication or corruption)
User-facing error messages do not leak internal schema/stack trace details
Median response time for a single-record read stays under 200ms at low concurrency (10 VUs)
p95 response time at moderate concurrency (50 VUs) stays under 2s for read-heavy workload
System degrades gracefully (errors, not silent data loss) under load beyond nominal capacity
Database connection pooling is present and configurable
N+1 query patterns are avoidable/avoided in the default data-access path for list endpoints
Pagination is supported and enforced by default on list endpoints (no unbounded result sets)
supabase_justification: GET /rest/v1/records returns a Content-Range header (e.g. 0-999/*) and caps the response at 1000 rows by default (PostgREST's default max-rows), even with no explicit Range/limit param supplied by the client. Clients paginate further via the Range header.
django_justification: Confirmed via the SQL-injection probe response and a direct list call (Section 7 hands-on checks, 2026-08-14): GET /records/ returns the entire in-org record set (hundreds of accumulated rows from benchmark test data) as a bare, unbounded JSON array — no Content-Range-equivalent metadata, no page/limit wrapper. DRF pagination classes were never configured.

criterion: API follows a documented, standard convention (REST/OpenAPI) that third-party HTTP clients can consume without custom SDKs
System can coexist with other services sharing the same database/infrastructure without conflict
supabase_justification: Supabase officially exposes a direct Postgres connection string (Settings > Database) specifically so other tools (BI/analytics, ORMs, cron jobs) can connect to the same underlying database alongside the Supabase-managed API layer.
django_justification: The db container is a standard postgres:16 instance reachable by any other service on the same Docker network or via an exposed port; nothing about the schema or RLS-free setup prevents additional consumers.

criterion: Standard authentication tooling (e.g. Postman, curl, standard OAuth/JWT libraries) works against the API without provider-specific plugins
Client libraries/SDKs are available in more than one language/ecosystem
supabase_justification: Official/community client libraries exist for JavaScript/TypeScript, Python, Flutter/Dart, Swift, Kotlin, C#, Go, Ruby, and GDScript (supabase.com/docs/guides/api/rest/client-libs).
django_justification: No official generated client library ships with this implementation — it's a plain DRF REST API, consumable from any language's standard HTTP client, but nothing is officially provided or maintained the way Supabase's typed SDKs are.

criterion: API versioning strategy exists and is documented
supabase_justification: The REST endpoint is nominally versioned in its URL (/rest/v1/), but this reflects the platform's PostgREST version, not application-level API versioning. Supabase's documented recommendation for versioning your own schema/breaking changes is to use separate Postgres schemas (e.g. v1, v2) with postgrest-js's schema switch — a real strategy, but manual and not enforced by the platform.
django_justification: No versioning strategy (URL, header, or otherwise) was configured for this reference implementation; DRF supports several versioning schemes out of the box, but none was set up in this build.

criterion: Documentation/dashboard is understandable to a developer without prior platform-specific experience within a reasonable ramp-up (subjective, state your own ramp-up time)
Common administrative tasks (e.g. viewing a table's rows, checking a policy) are reachable within a small, countable number of clicks/commands
Error messages returned to a developer/operator are actionable (state what's wrong and how to fix it)
Setup/onboarding requires no undocumented manual steps beyond what the platform's own quickstart describes
Dashboard/admin UI is available out of the box without custom development
Accessibility of any provided dashboard UI (keyboard navigation, screen-reader labels) meets a basic bar
System recovers automatically from a transient database connection loss without manual intervention
A crashed worker/process is automatically restarted without operator action
Data is durably persisted across a full restart of all application containers/services
Automated backups exist and are documented, with a stated retention policy
supabase_justification: Daily backups and PITR are documented platform features, but NOT included at the Free/Nano tier this project actually uses (Defense_Arguments.md entry 7's compute-budget decision). Daily backups start at the Pro tier ($25/mo, 7-day retention); PITR is a paid add-on requiring at least a Small compute tier. At the tier actually benchmarked, no automated backup is running.
django_justification: No automated backup mechanism (cron pg_dump, VPS snapshot schedule, etc.) was configured for this reference implementation; Postgres data persists only via the Docker volume, which is not itself a backup strategy.

criterion: A documented, testable disaster-recovery/restore procedure exists
supabase_justification: Supabase publishes a general restore procedure for PITR/daily backups via the Dashboard, but no project-specific restore was actually tested during this build — and per the row above, the tier used doesn't have backups enabled to restore from in the first place.
django_justification: No disaster-recovery procedure was documented or tested for this implementation; restoring would mean manually recreating the Docker volume from a pg_dump that was never scheduled to begin with.

criterion: Uptime/SLA commitment is published (or, for self-hosted, is a function of the chosen VPS provider's published SLA)
supabase_score: Not satisfied at the tier used
supabase_justification: Supabase's 99.9% uptime SLA (supabase.com/sla) is contractually available only on the Enterprise plan (custom pricing, effectively ~$25,000+/year). Free, Pro, and Team customers have no contractual uptime commitment at all — this project runs on the Free tier, so there is no SLA in practice, only the platform's general reliability.
django_score: Pending — depends on final VPS choice (§4.11, not yet provisioned)
django_justification: Formal SLA availability varies sharply by provider: DigitalOcean publishes a 99.99% SLA, Linode/Akamai offers an enterprise-grade SLA, but Hetzner publishes no formal uptime SLA at all (independently observed ~99.95%, no compensation mechanism). Score depends on which provider is actually selected in §4.11.

criterion: System exposes health-check/status endpoints suitable for external monitoring
supabase_justification: Not meaningfully testable at the application level; Supabase's own infrastructure health is monitored platform-side (status.supabase.com), not through a project-specific endpoint. Note this asymmetry rather than scoring it as a deficiency.
django_justification: Checked /health, /healthz, /api/health, /api/health/ — all returned 404. No health-check endpoint was built for this implementation; an operator would need to add one (e.g. a trivial DB-ping view) before production use.

criterion: Migration/schema-change failures are transactional (all-or-nothing, no partial schema state left behind)
All API endpoints require authentication by default (no accidental public exposure)
supabase_justification: Every unauthenticated request made throughout the build/test process returned 401/403; no endpoint was reachable without a valid Bearer token.
django_justification: Same — custom UserAccountJWTAuthentication + DRF permission classes reject all unauthenticated requests.

criterion: Row-level authorisation is enforced at the data layer, not only in application code
supabase_justification: RLS policies enforced directly by Postgres, independent of any application-layer code — verified by the infinite-recursion and report_view fixes, both database-level changes.
django_justification: Enforcement is at the application layer (permission classes + queryset filtering), not the Postgres layer — no RLS on the Django-managed tables. An honest architectural asymmetry worth naming directly rather than obscuring: a bug in a Django view could bypass authorisation in a way an RLS bug at the DB layer generally cannot.

criterion: Malformed or tampered JWTs are rejected with a generic error, no internal detail leaked
supabase_justification: Verified via pytest and manual curl testing across Section 5; malformed tokens return 401 without stack traces or internal detail.
django_justification: Same verification method, same result.

criterion: Expired tokens are rejected and cannot be used to authenticate further requests
supabase_justification: Encountered directly during testing — the default 1-hour Supabase token expiry caused real 401s mid-session, correctly rejected.
django_justification: Encountered directly — the default 5-minute SIMPLE_JWT access-token lifetime caused real 401s mid-session before being extended to 24h for testing convenience; expiry enforcement itself worked correctly at both settings.

criterion: Server-derived fields (e.g. created_by, org_id) cannot be overridden by client-supplied payload values
supabase_justification: Initial build allowed client-supplied created_by, enabling authorship spoofing (Defense_Arguments.md entry 4); fixed via DB column DEFAULT auth.uid() plus a strengthened WITH CHECK policy; re-verified via pytest.
django_justification: RecordSerializer already excluded org/created_by from client input via read_only_fields; perform_create() derives both server-side.

criterion: Password storage uses a modern, salted, adaptive hashing algorithm (not reversible encryption)
supabase_justification: Supabase Auth (GoTrue) hashes passwords with bcrypt plus a per-password random salt, stored in auth.users.encrypted_password (supabase.com/docs/guides/auth/password-security).
django_justification: Django's default password hasher is PBKDF2 with SHA256 and a per-password salt — modern and adaptive (configurable work factor); this implementation did not override Django's default, and did not add django[argon2] which would be the stronger alternative if desired.

criterion: All traffic is served over TLS by default, with plaintext HTTP disabled or redirected
Sensitive configuration (API keys, DB credentials) is never present in client-side/browser-reachable code or responses
Rate limiting or equivalent abuse protection exists on authentication endpoints
SQL injection is not possible via any parameterised/filterable API input
supabase_justification: Supabase-side probe inconclusive this run — JWT expired before this check executed; needs a re-run with a fresh token before final scoring.
django_justification: Injection payload (?id=1' OR '1'='1) in a query filter had no effect on the executed query — Django REST Framework/ORM parameterises all queryset filtering, so the malformed param was simply not recognised as a valid filter and the endpoint fell back to its default (unfiltered) queryset rather than executing any injected SQL.

criterion: File upload endpoints reject executable/script file types by default or via explicit configuration
File uploads are stored outside the web-servable document root (or equivalent isolation for object storage)
Session/token invalidation on logout is immediate and verifiable (token cannot be reused after logout)
supabase_justification: Logout call succeeded (204), but the same access token still worked on a subsequent request (200) — the logout revokes the server-side session/refresh token, not the already-issued short-lived access token, since GoTrue JWTs are stateless and not checked against a revocation list on every request. A functioning logout endpoint exists (unlike Django), but it does not achieve immediate access-token invalidation.
django_justification: No logout/blacklist endpoint exists in this implementation; reusing the token after the client discarded it still returned 200. SIMPLE_JWT has no token-blacklist app configured, so issued tokens remain valid until natural expiry regardless of any client-side logout action. Net effect is the same as Supabase's (token survives 'logout') but for a more basic reason — no logout endpoint was built at all, vs. Supabase's endpoint existing but not covering access-token revocation.

criterion: Multi-factor authentication is available as an option for user accounts
supabase_justification: TOTP (authenticator app) and phone/SMS MFA are built into Supabase Auth and free to use on every plan including Free, via the standard Enroll/Challenge/Verify API (supabase.com/docs/guides/auth/auth-mfa). Organization-wide MFA *enforcement* requires Pro+, but the capability for a user to opt into MFA is available regardless of tier.
django_justification: No MFA was implemented in this reference implementation; adding it would require an additional package (e.g. django-otp) and is not part of djangorestframework-simplejwt out of the box.

criterion: Security-relevant events (failed logins, permission denials) are logged in a form usable for audit
Logs do not contain full request bodies with sensitive data (PII, credentials) by default
CORS policy is explicit and does not default to wildcard-allow-all in a production configuration
supabase_justification: An OPTIONS preflight from an arbitrary, untrusted origin (https://evil-example.com) received access-control-allow-origin: * — wildcard by default, permitting any origin to make browser-based requests given a valid API key/token.
django_justification: The same preflight from an untrusted origin returned no Access-Control-Allow-Origin header at all — no CORS middleware is configured, so browsers block cross-origin requests by default. This technically satisfies the criterion, but it's a side effect of CORS never being configured rather than a deliberate restrictive policy; a legitimate frontend on a different origin would also be blocked and would need explicit configuration (e.g. django-cors-headers) to work at all.

criterion: Security headers (e.g. HSTS, X-Content-Type-Options) are present on API responses
supabase_justification: strict-transport-security and x-content-type-options are present by default (platform-managed). No X-Frame-Options or Content-Security-Policy header observed, though both are of limited relevance to a JSON-only API surface (no HTML rendered).
django_justification: X-Frame-Options: DENY and X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff are present (Django's default SecurityMiddleware). No Strict-Transport-Security header — expected while testing over plain HTTP on localhost; would need to be verified again against a real TLS-terminated deployment (§4.11) before scoring this row as final.

criterion: Dependency/package vulnerabilities are surfaced by an available scanning mechanism (platform-provided or addable)
supabase_justification: Application code is not user-maintained (no requirements.txt/package.json for the deployed backend itself); dependency security is Supabase's operational responsibility, not something scored against a self-run scan.
django_justification: pip-audit against requirements.txt found 12 known CVEs across 3 packages: django 4.2.30 (6 CVEs, fixed in 5.2.15+/6.0.x), urllib3 1.26.20 (5 CVEs, fixed in 2.5.0-2.7.0), python-dotenv 1.2.1 (1 CVE, fixed in 1.2.2). The scanning mechanism itself is satisfied — it's available, free, and worked — but the findings are a real, disclosed limitation: dependencies should be bumped before final submission/production use.

criterion: Business-logic constraints (e.g. a record cannot belong to two organisations) are enforced server-side, not just in the client
supabase_justification: org_id is server-derived (see created_by row above) and RLS additionally scopes every query; a record cannot be associated with an org the caller doesn't belong to.
django_justification: org is server-derived via perform_create() and get_queryset() filtering; same guarantee enforced server-side.

criterion: Administrative/privileged operations require a distinct, more strongly authenticated credential than standard user operations
Input length/size limits are enforced to prevent resource-exhaustion via oversized payloads
supabase_justification: POST with a 500,000-character string in the title field was rejected (400) rather than accepted — the underlying Postgres column type/constraint enforces a limit.
django_justification: POST with a 500,000-character string in a text field returned 201 Created with no rejection or truncation — no field-level or request-level size limit is enforced.

criterion: Direct object references (e.g. record IDs) cannot be enumerated to access other organisations' data
supabase_justification: Explicitly covered by the cross-org record ID tests in test_authorization.py (OTHER_ORG_RECORD_ID fixture), 12/12 passing — a known other-org record ID returns 200+[] (empty), not the record.
django_justification: Same test suite, same fixture — a known other-org record ID returns 404, not the record.

criterion: Secrets rotation (API keys, DB passwords) is possible without downtime
supabase_justification: This project's Supabase instance uses the newer asymmetric API-key/signing-key system (confirmed via the dashboard's JWT Signing Keys UI encountered earlier in this build). Under that system, publishable and secret keys can be rotated instantly without invalidating existing user sessions. (Note: the legacy shared-secret JWT system, still in use by older Supabase projects, does NOT support this — regenerating the JWT secret there immediately invalidates all issued keys/sessions.)
django_justification: Rotating DB_PASSWORD means updating django-variant/.env and restarting the web/db containers — a brief service interruption in this simple docker-compose setup, since there's no rolling-restart or connection-draining mechanism configured. A production setup would need multiple replicas or a managed DB to avoid this.

criterion: Threat-modelling or security-architecture documentation is available for the platform's own infrastructure (BaaS) or was produced for this deployment (self-hosted)
supabase_justification: Supabase publishes general platform security/compliance documentation, but no project-specific threat model was produced for this deployment beyond the ad-hoc findings logged during the build (RLS recursion, view security_invoker, authorship spoofing — Defense_Arguments.md entries 2-4).
django_justification: No formal threat-modelling document was produced for this deployment either, but the same ad-hoc security findings during the build (server-derived fields, RLS-layer absence noted at row 41) functionally constitute informal threat analysis, even though it wasn't organised as a structured document (e.g. STRIDE).

criterion: Codebase is organised into clearly separable modules/layers (data access, business logic, API surface)
A change to one endpoint's validation logic does not require touching unrelated modules
Automated test suite exists and covers the core authorisation logic
assessment_method: Hands-on verification (Section 5, this guide's own test suite)
supabase_justification: 12 cross-target integration tests (test_authorization.py + test_equivalence.py) exercise RLS and permission boundaries directly; all passing.
django_justification: Same 12 integration tests plus 4 Django-specific unit tests; all passing.

criterion: Test suite can be run in a single command with no manual setup beyond documented steps
supabase_justification: pytest tests/ (with tests/config.py sourcing .env) runs the full cross-target suite in one command.
django_justification: Same command for integration tests; docker compose run --rm web pytest for the Django-specific unit tests.

criterion: Static analysis / linting is configured and passes cleanly
Code changes can be reviewed via a standard diff (not exclusively through a proprietary dashboard UI)
Business logic that would traditionally live in Edge Functions/serverless functions is inspectable and version-controllable as plain source, not only configured through a dashboard
supabase_justification: No Edge Functions were built for this implementation (Defense_Arguments.md entry 1 — RLS was judged sufficient for this application's business logic). RLS policies themselves are version-controlled SQL migrations, but Auth/Storage configuration was done via the dashboard, not fully expressed as code.
django_justification: All business logic is plain Python under version control; no dashboard-only configuration path exists for application logic.

criterion: A new developer can trace a request from API entry point to database query without needing platform-specific internal knowledge
Lines of code and dependency count are known and documented for the implementation (Section 5.4/Table 5.4)
Database schema changes are tracked in version control as migrations, not only as live dashboard edits
supabase_justification: Initial schema was migration-tracked (0001-0003), but several fixes this session (RLS recursion fix, security_invoker view fix, created_by default) were applied live via the SQL Editor rather than committed migration files. Should be backfilled into migration files before final submission for full compliance — noted here rather than silently left inconsistent.
django_justification: All schema changes went through makemigrations/migrate and are fully tracked in version control.

criterion: Test coverage percentage is measurable and reported
Application can run against a different underlying Postgres provider (self-hosted, different cloud) without code changes
Full data export (schema + data) is possible in a standard format (e.g. pg_dump) without provider-specific tooling
supabase_justification: Both variants are plain PostgreSQL databases; pg_dump works identically against either. Supabase also exposes a direct Postgres connection string for this purpose (Settings > Database), not requiring the Supabase CLI.
django_justification: Same — django-variant's db container is unmodified postgres:16; pg_dump requires no Django-specific tooling.

criterion: Application container/runtime can be installed on a fresh environment following only the documented steps in this guide
Switching to a different auth provider is possible without a full application rewrite
supabase_justification: Supabase publishes official migration guides for Auth0, AWS Cognito, and Firebase Auth, and supports running Supabase Auth alongside a third-party provider during migration to avoid disruption. Supabase Auth (GoTrue) is itself open-source and self-hostable, which further reduces lock-in risk.
django_justification: Authentication is a thin, explicitly custom layer (UserAccountJWTAuthentication + djangorestframework-simplejwt); swapping to a different provider means replacing one authentication backend class, not a framework-level rewrite.

criterion: Switching to a different object-storage backend is possible without a full application rewrite
supabase_justification: Supabase Storage exposes an S3-compatible API, so the underlying files/buckets can be moved to another S3-compatible provider — but the storage.objects metadata table, its RLS policies, and any Supabase-Storage-specific client calls are platform-specific and would need to be rebuilt against the new backend, not just re-pointed.
django_justification: django-storages (S3Boto3Storage, configured in §4.6) already abstracts the storage backend behind Django's standard storage API; swapping providers (or backend type entirely — filesystem, GCS, Azure) is a settings.py configuration change, not a code rewrite.

criterion: No proprietary, non-standard SQL extensions are required for the application's core schema/queries to function
supabase_justification: Row-Level Security (SECURITY DEFINER functions, RLS policies) is a standard PostgreSQL 9.5+ feature, not a Supabase-proprietary extension — the schema would run unmodified on any plain Postgres instance.
django_justification: No extensions used beyond core PostgreSQL/Django ORM features.

criterion: Local development environment can be run entirely offline/without a live cloud account (self-hosted) vs. requires live cloud connectivity (BaaS) — document this asymmetry, don't score it as a deficiency for either side
Vendor lock-in risk is explicitly assessable: estimated effort (hours) to migrate away from the current provider/stack
Time from zero to a working authenticated CRUD endpoint (first successful request) is measured and documented
assessment_method: Hands-on, self-reported (from this guide's own build timeline)

criterion: Number of discrete manual dashboard/console configuration steps required (vs. steps expressible as code/CLI)
Number of distinct services/processes an operator is responsible for keeping running (self-hosted) vs. zero (BaaS)
Monthly direct cost at each of the three usage scenarios in Table 3.3 is known and documented
Overage/scaling cost behaviour beyond the base tier is documented (linear, stepped, or unpredictable)
supabase_justification: Overage is per-resource metered at published per-unit rates beyond each plan's included allowance: database storage $0.125/GB, egress $0.09/GB beyond 250GB included, file storage $0.021/GB, and $0.00325 per monthly active user. Predictable and linear, but egress and MAU are the two meters most likely to surprise a growing app, since both scale with usage rather than storage.
django_justification: VPS pricing is flat/fixed per compute tier (e.g. DigitalOcean/Hetzner/Linode droplet pricing), not usage-metered — cost is a step function of the chosen tier rather than a continuous function of load, until bandwidth caps are exceeded (typically generous, several TB included per most providers). This fixed-vs-metered distinction is itself a core TCO finding for Table 5.3, not just a documentation note.

criterion: Estimated monthly operational effort (hours) for patching, monitoring, and backups is documented
